c-0ea4c10e6e.nodeLabel: DoDD 5205.07, Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (1 Jul 2010, Chg 2 of 4 Feb 2020)
c-0ea4c10e6e.text: CONGRESS KEEPS NOTHING. Para 4.h verbatim: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody. No copies shall be stored outside DoD repositories or control without the approval of the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' A briefed chairman therefore retains no document, no notes in committee custody, and no institutional memory once he leaves the chair.

c-127bc39a52.nodeLabel: Acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived - the three states of a DoD SAP
c-127bc39a52.text: DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.f makes the nesting operative: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security.' Waived is a strict subset of unacknowledged; there is no such thing as a waived acknowledged SAP.

c-148a97616f.text: 32 CFR 117.3(b) defines ACCM verbatim: 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.' ACCM is thus a SAP-like access control that by definition sits outside the SAP reporting statutes.

c-1b4d83fb74.nodeLabel: Cover mechanisms - HVSACO, nicknames, unacknowledged locations
c-1b4d83fb74.text: THE UNCLASSIFIED WITHHOLDING. DoDM 5205.07 Vol 1, Enclosure 5, para 1 lists when HVSACO is applied, including '(4) To protect information that does not warrant classification under Executive Order 13526' and '(5) When using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged SAP.' HVSACO is therefore a control expressly designed to hold inside SAP channels material that does NOT meet the standard for classification. Para 1.c requires that on a public release request the originator review the material and either remove the HVSACO marking or 'Inform the requestor of the decision not to release the information, citing an appropriate authority.'

c-1fff6fcd25.text: Mace asked whether material is given to particular contractors because of their expertise, offering General Dynamics for undersea propulsion; Elizondo answered 'Yes, ma'am, absolutely correct.'

c-255631b086.text: THE CAP-TO-SAP LAUNDERING BAR. Sec. 6603 adds 50 U.S.C. 3091a(b)(2)(A), verbatim: 'Except as provided in subparagraph (B), a head of an element of the intelligence community may not transfer a capability from a controlled access program, including from a compartment or subcompartment therein to a compartment or subcompartment of another controlled access program, to a special access program (as defined in section 1152(g) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1994 (50 U.S.C. 3348(g))), or to anything else outside the controlled access program, until the head submits to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership notice of the intent of the head to make such transfer.' Text at 138 STAT. 2507-2508.

c-267f7f10ba.text: HISTORICAL CORROBORATION FROM A CONGRESSIONALLY CHARTERED COMMISSION. The Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (1997), Chapter II, states verbatim: 'Among black programs, further distinction is made for "waived" programs, considered to be so sensitive that they are exempt from standard reporting requirements to the Congress. The chairperson, ranking member, and, on occasion, other members and staff of relevant Congressional committees are notified only orally of the existence of these programs.' The same passage gives the surrounding population: 'There are approximately 150 DoD-approved SAPs (the exact number is classified and others have been created but not yet formally approved), down from 200 in the late 1980s, and roughly 300 SCI compartments, compared with an estimated 800 in the late 1980s.' The Commission gives no number for the waived subset. The phrase 'notified only orally' is the operationally important one: it describes a practice under which the 119(e)(2) delivery leaves no paper.

c-4a265653bd.nodeLabel: Waived unacknowledged special access program (waived USAP)
c-4a265653bd.text: The combination that produces a genuinely invisible program is not one provision but three stacked: 119(e) removes the content from the written record; the sec. 1061 Pub. L. 114-328 sunset (eff. 31 Dec 2021) removed the annual census that would otherwise show a count; and the DoDD 5205.07 carve-out provision (see 32 CFR 117.6) removes DCSA from the contractor facility where the work is performed. Each layer is individually lawful and documented; the stack is what defeats discovery. Reasoning stated.

c-b8658d10cc.text: GAO HAS DESCRIBED THE WAIVER MECHANISM BUT HAS NEVER PUBLICLY REPORTED AN INSTANCE OF ITS USE. GAO/NSIAD-93-78, the unclassified summary of a classified report, describes the mechanism verbatim: 'Section 119, 10 U.S. Code, enacted in 1987, requires DOD to submit annual reports to the congressional defense committees on special access programs. Under the law, the Secretary of Defense may waive the requirement that certain information on special access programs be included in the annual report if he determines that the inclusion would adversely affect national security. However, he must provide the excluded information to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.' The report then never returns to the subject. Its findings on waivers are about a different thing entirely - 'DOD used waivers and exemptions to limit review, documentation, and reporting requirements' refers to Defense Acquisition Board reviews, competition requirements and Selected Acquisition Reports, not to Section 119(e). Do not let these two senses of 'waiver' be conflated on the board.

claimed.text: The board infers from these standing review and delegation rules that waived programmes exist, since a department does not write such rules for an empty set; no instance is public.

Representative Mace said at a public hearing that only certain people know the name of the programme and that if you do not know it you cannot get the information. She also asked whether material is given to particular contractors for their expertise, and Luis Elizondo said yes, absolutely correct.

On the board's reading, a legacy recovery and exploitation effort would map onto the taxonomy as a waived unacknowledged operations and support programme, covering custody of property, with an acquisition compartment for exploitation under the same umbrella; and the allegation reduces to whether the waiver was used or the activity was never entered into the SAP system at all.

The board infers that three stacked provisions produce a genuinely invisible programme: the waiver removes the content, the 2021 sunset removed the annual count, and the carve-out removes the outside inspector. It also infers that HVSACO material sits outside the declassification system entirely, and that ACCM triggers no congressional notice under any of the four reporting statutes.

The board reads the 2024 reissue as relocating rather than abolishing the architecture, moving it one document down the hierarchy, and notes that the regulation still points at a directive that no longer defines the carve-out. It reads the contractor rule in paragraph 4.e as a gag, since the approving office is the subject of the disclosure.
The board infers that a complete list of waived programmes exists as an agency record, because it is reviewed and validated every year.

The board also sets DARPA beside the category as the open counterfactual, with named programme managers and a public budget, reads CENTER LANE as a ridiculed subject held under service-secretary-level access controls, and reads HVSACO and nickname practice as the paperwork environment Elizondo has described.

contested.text: DoD states that Elizondo had no assigned responsibilities for AATIP while in OUSD(I), that DIA administered AATIP, and that he interacted with the DIA office managing it but did not lead it.

No public document identifies a single waived programme, a count, a date or any connection to unidentified anomalous phenomena, and a search across GAO, Inspector General, CRS and Armed Services Committee material found no UAP-specific use of the waiver.
The Department's instruction says waived programmes remain subject to congressional oversight.
The documented UAP-related SAP request, relating to AATIP in November 2009, was recommended against by USD(I) James Clapper.

The records disagree on who sees a waived programme: the board's own waived-programme entry speaks of an eight-member floor, while the statute sends the material to the chairman and ranking member of each of the six defense committees, which another entry counts as twelve.
The public texts disagree on whether the three states still exist: the 2024 directive's definitions omit them, while the instruction issued the same day keeps them.
CENTER LANE is not evidence of a waived programme: no opened record connects it to waived status or to any unacknowledged programme.

lead.text: The Department of Defense sorts special access programmes into three states: acknowledged, whose existence is known but whose details are classified; unacknowledged, whose existence itself is protected; and waived, a subset of unacknowledged programmes whose standard reporting to Congress the Secretary has waived. This topic covers the directives, manuals and regulation that define those states and the devices that keep the deeper ones out of sight.

notes: The three states of a special access programme and the DoD directives that define them; the core of the SAP-law community, split from reporting and governance because each answers a different question.
questions: How many waived programmes are on the list the Senior Review Group reviews each year, and has any ever concerned the subject of this board?
How do the 2024 categories, the Joint Force Integration SAP and the Strategic Enabler SAP, map onto the older acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived states?
Has any UAP-related material been held under the HVSACO caveat, outside the classification system?
Was the 2009 special access programme request relating to AATIP ever approved in any form?
What do Volumes 2 to 4 of the SAP Security Manual now say, given that the live copies are no longer retrievable?
Is any UAP-related information protected under Alternative Compensatory Control Measures rather than as a special access programme?

record.text: The 2010 directive, cleared for public release, reissued the 2006 directive, and restated the waiver as policy: where the Secretary determines that reporting to Congress by standard processes would adversely affect national security, he or she may designate select unacknowledged programmes as waived under 10 U.S.C. 119.

The same directive limited waived programmes, absent the Secretary's or Deputy Secretary's approval, to the chair, ranking minority member and staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees; kept all waived material submitted to Congress in DoD custody; required timely notice to SAPCO when briefing Congress; barred contractors from giving SAP material to Congress without SAPCO's approval; and denied members' personal staff any access.

It also subjected everyone with access to a random counterintelligence-scope polygraph, required SAPCO to seek the Deputy Secretary's approval each year of the billet structure covering every DoD programme, and routed access for the White House, the NSC, political appointees and, for waived programmes, judicial personnel through SAPCO.

The 2024 directive, approved by Deputy Secretary Hicks, cancels the 2010 one and incorporates the July 2023 SAP Enterprise Reform guidance. It says new umbrellas and compartments will be established by exception, with the Secretary's or Deputy Secretary's approval, keeps the Oversight Committee as the senior governing body, and makes SAPCO the primary point of contact with the legislative branch.

The DoD SAP Security Manual comes in four volumes: general procedures, personnel security, physical security and marking. Volume 1 folded the former overprint to the industrial security manual supplement into a public manual, and it survives in full only in Internet Archive captures, its live paths returning 404.

The manual's HVSACO caveat exists to keep general programme information inside acknowledged and unacknowledged SAP channels and to minimise operational security indicators. It is applied, among other cases, to information that does not warrant classification under EO 13526 and whenever a nickname for an unacknowledged programme is used; the manual says it is not a classification, and on a release request the originator either removes it or tells the requester the information will not be released.

Every programme must carry an unclassified nickname generated under the Joint Chiefs' nickname manual, and those nicknames are what the annual report to Congress uses. The manual also bars the use of government identification cards in unacknowledged locations, and lets several programmes, including carved-out ones, share one facility under a co-utilisation agreement.

32 CFR 117 defines Alternative Compensatory Control Measures as security measures used where normal measures cannot achieve strict need-to-know and SAP controls are not required, and places them in the same supplement as SAPs, SCI and Restricted Data, applied through specific contract requirements. The rule implements EO 12829.

The 2010 glossary also defines the carve-out, the provision that relieves the Defense Security Service of industrial security oversight for a programme, and SAPCO holds the list of carved-out facilities.

DoDI 5205.11 provides that the Secretary may designate select unacknowledged programmes as waived, and it writes standing duties around them: the Oversight Committee reviews all waived programmes each year; the Senior Review Group reviews them annually and checks the accuracy of the list sent to Congress; SAPCO sets the review criteria; and the instruction has separate delegation rules for access approval on waived programmes.

Outside records confirm the category. The Moynihan Commission wrote in 1997 that waived programmes were considered so sensitive that they were exempt from standard reporting to Congress, and a 1994 commission noted that some of the most sensitive DoD programmes were waived or carved out.
GAO has described the waiver without reporting a use of it: GAO/NSIAD-93-78 set out the mechanism, and the earlier GAO/NSIAD-89-133 did not mention the section 119(e) waiver at all.

The waiver is a statutory term traced to one sentence, 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2), which sends the information and justification jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each defense committee and requires nothing written, retained or shared. The comparable waiver for other agencies in 50 U.S.C. 3348(e) still sends the information to the full oversight committees.

Representative Nancy Mace sits on House Armed Services, one of the six defense committees, but as neither chair nor ranking member she has no entitlement under section 119(e)(2) and would not be told a waiver had been used.

The CAPCO marking register gives special access programmes their own marking category, and since December 2024 the law bars transferring a capability from an intelligence controlled access programme to a special access programme until notice is submitted, subject to two exceptions.

The UAP funding bar of 2023 acts on the waived category without changing it: section 1687 conditions money for UAP activity under special or restricted access on disclosure to the committees and leadership, and does not amend section 119(e).

A documented moment where a visible UAP programme was considered for conversion is on paper: DIA's AAWSAP solicitation and statement of work of August 2008 are public, and an OUSD(I) information memorandum of November 2009 records the review of a special access programme request relating to AATIP.

Earlier instances show the states in operation. GAO's 1988 report is a primary statement of how programmes were established and by whom; NSDD 159 of 1985 ordered a special access compartment over a whole policy subject; and the Army's psychoenergetics work, begun as GRILL FLAME in 1977, ran as CENTER LANE, a Secretary of the Army designated special access programme with a category three access caveat, until INSCOM proposed ending it in July 1984; it was deactivated in March 1985 and its assets attached to DIA.

summary.text: The 2010 DoD directive defined the three states word for word, calling a waived programme an unacknowledged SAP with more restrictive reporting and access controls, and the 2024 instruction makes the nesting operative: only select unacknowledged programmes can be designated waived. Cutting across the states are categories by mission, such as acquisition programmes protecting research, development and procurement, and operations and support programmes protecting sensitive military operations, property and plans.

Every category descends from section 4.3 of EO 13526, and 32 CFR 117.3 gives the regulatory definition that binds contractors: a programme established to control access and distribution and to protect particularly sensitive classified information beyond that normally required at Top Secret, Secret or Confidential.

The 2024 reissue of the directive dropped the definitions of acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived programmes and of the carve-out, and added new categories such as the Joint Force Integration SAP and the Strategic Enabler SAP; the older taxonomy survives in the companion instruction.

Around the states sit cover devices and a lower tier: the HVSACO handling caveat, which is expressly not a classification, unclassified nicknames in the report to Congress, and Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, used where SAP controls are not required.

title: Special access programmes: acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived
